details.text:
Steps as text

Read Committed

Before the purchase, P7 has stock 1. The report opens a transaction. Neither report query has run.
The report’s first SELECT reads stock 1 from the committed state before checkout. Read 1 marks that view.
Checkout commits its purchase. The current stock is now 0. The report remains open; its first result does not change.
Read Committed takes a new snapshot for the second SELECT. It returns 0, including checkout’s commit.

Repeatable Read

Before the purchase, P7 has stock 1. The report opens a transaction. Neither report query has run.
The report’s first SELECT reads stock 1 from the committed state before checkout. Read 1 marks that view.
Checkout commits its purchase. The current stock is now 0. The report remains open; its first result does not change.
Repeatable Read uses the snapshot established by the first query. The second SELECT also returns 1, although checkout has committed stock 0.

Before the purchase, P7 has stock 1. The report opens a transaction. Neither report query has run.
The report’s first SELECT reads stock 1 from the committed state before checkout. Read 1 marks that view.
Checkout commits its purchase. The current stock is now 0. The report remains open; its first result does not change.
Repeatable Read uses the snapshot established by the first query. The second SELECT also returns 1, although checkout has committed stock 0.

Steps as text

Repeatable Read

Session S502 starts with Ada and Tomas both on duty. At least one instructor must remain.
Both transactions read the two on-duty rows before either changes one. Ada sees Tomas on; Tomas sees Ada on. Each decides that leaving would keep one instructor.
Ada sets her own row off duty and commits. The committed state now has only Tomas on duty. Tomas’s earlier read still says Ada was on.
Tomas changes a different row. Repeatable Read permits his update and commit in this schedule. No instructor remains on duty.
Ada relied on Tomas not having left; Tomas relied on Ada not having left. Both decisions cannot belong to any serial order. The rule is broken.
Two complete transactions and two stable snapshots have produced zero cover. A snapshot is not the same promise as a serial outcome.

Serializable

Session S502 starts with Ada and Tomas both on duty. At least one instructor must remain.
Both transactions read the two on-duty rows before either changes one. Ada sees Tomas on; Tomas sees Ada on. Each decides that leaving would keep one instructor.
Ada sets her own row off duty and commits. The committed state now has only Tomas on duty. Tomas’s earlier read still says Ada was on.
With both transactions Serializable, PostgreSQL rejects Tomas’s transaction in this schedule with SQLSTATE 40001. His change does not commit. Tomas remains on duty.
Tomas retries the whole transaction with a fresh snapshot and reruns the decision. Only Tomas is on duty now, so he must stay.
The fresh attempt commits without turning Tomas off. Ada is off, Tomas is on: the same result as Ada leaving first, followed by Tomas deciding to stay.

Success: borrow C, begin, reserve stock and write order, commit, return idle C. No stock: borrow, begin, receive zero rows, roll back all earlier work, return idle C. data.text:
Sources and further reading

Checked on 24 October 2026 against the PostgreSQL 18 documentation and an owned disposable PostgreSQL 18.6 instance. The fixed shop rows remain unchanged; tenant and deletion examples are labelled variants, and rejected writes are attempts rather than committed history. Figure 1 illustrates lookups implied by the declarations, not the order PostgreSQL executes its checks. No performance or other engine’s execution is claimed.

PostgreSQL, Constraints: row checks, required values, identities, composite references, deletion actions, missing reference components and indexes on referencing columns.
PostgreSQL, Index Uniqueness Checks: why a conflicting insertion waits and checks the first transaction’s outcome.
PostgreSQL, CREATE TABLE and SET CONSTRAINTS: declarations, supported deferral and forcing a pending check.
PostgreSQL, Row Security Policies: the separate question of which rows a runtime identity may access.
PostgreSQL, Error Codes and Transactions: identifying a refusal and recovering an explicit failed transaction.
On this site, History, correction and deletion: deciding what should be retained or removed; Transactions and isolation: preserving rules across concurrent changes.

Sources and further reading

Checked on 24 October 2026 against PostgreSQL 18 documentation and a disposable PostgreSQL 18.6 instance. Download the SQL experiment and run it in a disposable database with psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f joins-experiment.sql. It creates temporary tables, checks the incorrect and corrected results, and rolls back. The figures use the collection’s fixed rows; they do not run SQL or depict a chosen join algorithm.

PostgreSQL, Joined Tables: matching pairs, outer joins and the difference between an ON condition and a WHERE restriction.
PostgreSQL, WITH Queries: naming intermediate results and when the planner can fold them into a larger query.
PostgreSQL, Subquery Expressions: correlated EXISTS, NOT EXISTS and missing values in NOT IN.
PostgreSQL, SELECT DISTINCT, Aggregate Functions and Conditional Expressions: duplicate result rows, sums and COALESCE.

Sources and further reading

Checked on 24 October 2026 against the PostgreSQL 18 manual and a disposable PostgreSQL 18.6 instance. Download the SQL experiment and run psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f windows-experiment.sql in a disposable database. It builds temporary inputs, checks the grouped and window results, adds the two later tie rows only for the ordering examples, and rolls back. The figures illustrate those calculations rather than running a database in the page.

PostgreSQL, GROUP BY and HAVING and Aggregate Functions: grouping, counts, empty inputs and non-missing contributions.
PostgreSQL, Window Functions tutorial: retaining rows, partitions, window input and filtering at a later query level.
PostgreSQL, Window Functions: ranking, LAG, LAST_VALUE and frame-dependent behaviour.
PostgreSQL, Window Function Calls: explicit ROWS and RANGE frames; Aggregate Expressions: FILTER.
PostgreSQL, Sorting Rows: output order, directions and tie-breaking expressions.

Sources and further reading
PostgreSQL 18, LIMIT and OFFSET and Sorting Rows: unique ordering, skipped rows and the work required by an offset.
PostgreSQL, Row Constructor Comparison: left-to-right tuple comparison and missing fields; Date/Time Types: timestamp resolution and precision.
PostgreSQL, Transaction Isolation: statement and transaction snapshots; Sequence Manipulation Functions: sequence allocation outside transactional rollback.
PostgreSQL, DECLARE and FETCH: transaction cursors, held cursors and their materialisation.
PostgreSQL, Routine Vacuuming: dead versions retained for transactions that can still see them. Time, snapshots and distributed reads continues into snapshots across machines.

Sources and further reading
Psycopg 3, Passing parameters and SQL composition: value binding and identifiers.
Psycopg 3, Adapting Python types and Errors: returned values and structured error fields.
Psycopg 3, Transaction management, Connection pools and cancel_safe: the scopes and cancellation used here.
PostgreSQL 18, statement_timeout: what the server limit includes; Error Codes: stable error identities.
On this site, Connections, overload and capacity develops pool limits and waiting; Database access and least privilege develops the connection’s authority.

Sources and further reading

Checked on 24 October 2026 against the PostgreSQL 18 documentation and the disposable PostgreSQL 18.6 experiment. The article uses the collection’s fixed shop facts and its separate S502 instructor example. The interactive figures illustrate those decisions; they do not execute SQL in the browser.

PostgreSQL, Transactions and BEGIN: transaction blocks, atomic visibility, autocommit, rollback and savepoints.
PostgreSQL, Transaction Isolation: statement and transaction snapshots, Read Committed’s row recheck, Repeatable Read’s limits and Serializable’s read/write dependency checks.
PostgreSQL, Concurrency Control introduction and Row-Level Locks: row versions, ordinary readers and competing writers.
PostgreSQL, Serialization Failure Handling: 40001 and why a retry must rerun all of the transaction’s decision logic.
PostgreSQL, Check Constraints: the boundary between a row check and conditions involving other rows.
